name: Ivory Coast (Côte d’Ivoire)
summary: Independent from France in 1960; under Félix Houphouët-Boigny it became the world’s largest cocoa producer; civil wars followed in 2002–07 and 2010–11.

knownFor.label: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace
knownFor.note: One of the largest churches in the world.

location.value: West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea; 322,462 km².

terrain.value: Coastal lagoons and forests in the south, rolling savanna in the north and hills in the west.

climate.value: Tropical, humid in the south with two rainy seasons, and drier in the north.

resources.value: Cocoa (the world’s largest producer), coffee, oil, gold and timber.

disasters.value: Floods in Abidjan and coastal erosion are recurring problems.

population.value: 29,389,150 (2021 census, per the article); the text also gives 31.5 million for 2024.

urbanisation.value: Abidjan, the economic capital, has about 6 million people; Yamoussoukro is the political capital.

disease.value: Malaria and HIV are the main health problems, with outbreaks of yellow fever.

migration.value: Many workers from Burkina Faso and Mali.

economicBase.value: The world’s largest exporter of cocoa beans as of 2023 (the leading producer since 1979). Coffee output rose sharply after independence, making it third in the world behind Brazil and Colombia. The page gives no share of world output.

tradeRoutes.value: Cocoa and coffee leave through the port of Abidjan, which also serves landlocked Mali and Burkina Faso.

moneyAndTax.value: The West African CFA franc, shared with neighbours and pegged to the euro.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A unitary presidential republic; Parliament has a Senate and a 255-seat National Assembly.

succession.value: After the first president died in 1993 power passed to his successor, and the disputed 2010 election led to a brief civil war.

institutions.value: A presidency, National Assembly and Senate under a constitution revised in 2016.

stability.value: Military coup in late 1999 (Robert Guéï); civil war 2002–2007; second civil war in 2010–2011 after the 2010 presidential election.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A national army formed after the 2002–11 conflicts from government and rebel forces.

majorWars.value: First civil war 2002–2007 and second civil war 2010–2011. The page gives no overall death toll; it mentions 120 killed at a March 2004 opposition rally and hundreds killed in Duékoué.

territoryChange.value: The borders drawn by France have stayed the same since independence.

alliancesRivals.value: Close to France, which has a military base there, and a member of ECOWAS.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Universities in Abidjan and Bouaké; schooling has recovered after the war years.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: The Abidjan–Ouagadougou railway, built under French rule, links the port to Burkina Faso (completed 1954).

religion.value: 2021 census: Islam 42.5%, Christianity 39.8% (Catholic 17.0%), no religion 12.6%, traditional faiths 2.2%.

languageWriting.value: French is official; Dioula, Baoulé and many other languages are widely spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: Baoulé and Senufo masks and carvings, coupé-décalé music, and the huge basilica at Yamoussoukro (1989).

socialStructure.value: About 60 ethnic groups, with strong northern and southern regional identities.

sharedIdentity.value: Debates over “Ivoirité” (who counts as Ivorian) fuelled conflict.

dailyLife.value: Many families eat attiéké (cassava) and alloco (fried plantain), and farm small plots or work in towns.

neighbours.value: Liberia, Guinea, Mali, Burkina Faso, Ghana.

ideasReligions.value: French language and culture shaped the elite; Islam, Christianity and traditional beliefs are all widely held.

colonisation.value: A French colony (part of French West Africa) until 1960.

riseSignals.value: A French protectorate from 1843 and colony from 1893; independence on 7 August 1960.

peakPeriod.value: The “Ivorian miracle” of the 1960s–70s, when cocoa and coffee exports raised incomes rapidly.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Ivory Coast continues as an independent republic.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
